name: Duncan Lustig-Prean
train_texts: The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy on the sole ground that they are homosexual constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Government, represented by Mr M. Eaton and, subsequently, by Mr C. Whomersley, submitted their observations on 17 October 1997, to which the applicants replied on 20 November and 8 December 1997. The Commission decided to adjourn the applications pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome by the English High Court. The application was brought by Mr Lustig-Prean and Mr Beckett. The application was dismissed by the High Court in July 1998. The High Court withdrew its reference to the case after the decision of the ECJ in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins (13 July 1998) The applications were examined by the Third Section of the Court. On 4 May 1999 the President of the Chamber decided to grant the applicants legal aid. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. The Court heard addresses by D. Pannick QC, Mr J. Bowers QC and Ms J. Pfieffer. The first applicant joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. He was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately twenty minutes. The applicant was asked repeatedly about who had tipped him off that he was the subject of an investigation by the servicePolice. The search was normally completed but the applicant had already cleared his cabin. The case was heard at the Royal Court of Arbitration for Human Rights in London. The jury found that Mr Lustig-Prean was not entitled to apply for promotion to commander. The decision was made to reject his application for promotion. The second applicant joined the Royal Navy, enlisting for twenty-two years’ service. In 1991 he became a substantive weapons engineering mechanic. In December 1994 the Admiralty Board informed the applicant that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. The applicant’s commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000). His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal.  applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) and consequently he spoke with the chaplain, to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. On 10 May 1993 the applicant was asked by his lieutenant-commander to repeat what he had told the Chaplain and he again admitted his homosexuality to that officer. He was then called for interview by the service police and cautioned in the same terms as the first applicant. He would not be questioned on the above admissions prior to a search of his locker. His consent to the search was requested and given. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. The applicant was then questioned about his first and current homosexual relationship which began in December 1992. The service police report noted that the applicant, in openly declaring his homosexuality and his relationship with a civilian, had effectively disposed “of any immediate potential security concern” For that reason, it was considered in the report that “no cause was identified for conducting a security interview with Beckett” The Admiralty Board dismissed the applicant’s complaint. The applicants’ judicial review proceedings (R.C. v. Ministry of Defence, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) were heard in the High Court on 7 June 1995. On 28 July 1993 the applicant's administrative discharge was approved on the basis of his homosexuality. Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. He noted that the cases illustrated the hardships resulting from the absolute policy against homosexuals in the armed forces. All four of the applicants had exemplary service records, some with reports written in glowing terms. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” However, having considered arguments as to the test to be applied in the context of these judicial review proceedings, Simon Brown LJ concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles should be applied. Simon Brown LJ also found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals into the armed services. It followed that the applications had to be rejected “albeit with hesitation and regret”. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom”s obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. He pointed out that, although he might have considered the Minister wrong, “…[the courts] owe a duty ... to remain within their constitutional bounds and not trespass beyond them” In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to ‘management’ levels in the armed forces. The only countries operating a blanket ban were Turkey and Luxembourg (and, possibly, Portugal and Greece) The applicants in the judicial review proceedings had argued that the Ministry’s position was “bereft of factual evidence’. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment (with which the two other judges of the Court. of Appeal agreed) The more substantial the interference with human rights, the more the court will require by way of justification before it is satisfied that the decision is reasonable. Master of the Rolls: The greater the policy content of the decision and the more remote the subject matter of a decision from ordinary judicial experience, the more hesitant the court had to be in holding a decision to be irrational. He concluded that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed in this case. “The court must properly defer to the expertise of responsible decision-makers, it must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people’ …” Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls. He held that to dismiss a person from his or her employment on the grounds of a private sexual preference would not appear to show respect for that person’s private and family life. He questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights with which the primary adjudicating role on the Convention lay. Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments and, in particular, with the views expressed on the rationality test to be applied. In December 1995 Mr Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. On 19 March 1996 the Appeals Committee of the House of Lords refused leave to appeal to the Lords. Mr Beckett requested the withdrawal of his Industrial Tribunal proceedings and those proceedings were dismissed on 25 April 1996. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the. withdrawal of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed by the. Industrial Tribunal. The policy was, in his view, “ripe for review and for consideration of its replacement by a strict conduct code’.

The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The applications were adjourned pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome by the English High Court on the question of the applicability of the Council Directive on the Implementation of the Principle of Equal Treatment for Men and Women as regards Access to Employment, Vocational Training and Promotion and Working Conditions. The High Court delivered its judgment withdrawing its reference of the above question given the decision of the ECJ in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins (13 July 1998) On 4 May 1999 the President of the Chamber decided to grant Mr Lustig-Prean legal aid. The hearing in this case and in the. case of Smith and Grady v the United Kingdom took place in public in the Human Rights. Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Eadie, Counsel, and Ms J. Betteley, Adviser. Mr Lustig-Prean joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. He became a midshipman in the executive branch of the navy in 1983. His evaluation of November 1989 noted that he was an officer with ‘great potential’ In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. The applicant was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately twenty minutes. The first applicant (the first applicant) had been involved in a steady relationship with a civilian partner for about thirty months prior to June 1994. He was asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject) The second applicant joined the Royal Navy in 1989. In 1991 he became a substantive weapons engineering mechanic. On 16 December 1994 the Admiralty Board informed the applicant that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. The applicant’s commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000). His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. The second applicant is still serving in the Navy. In May 1993 the applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. On 10 May 1993 he was asked by his lieutenant-commander to repeat what he had told the chaplain. He again admitted his homosexuality to that officer and was then called for interview by the service police. He was cautioned in the same terms as the first applicant and told that he would not be questioned on the above admissions prior to a search of his locker. His consent to the search was requested and given. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. The service police report noted that the applicant, in openly declaring his homosexuality and his relationship with a civilian, had effectively disposed ‘of any immediate potential security concern’ The applicants’ judicial review proceedings (R.C. v. Ministry of Defence, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) were dismissed in December 1994. The applicants argued that the policy of the Ministry of. Defence against homosexuals in the armed forces was “irrational”, that it was in breach of the Convention and that it. was contrary to the Equal Treatment Directive. The. applicants obtained leave to apply for judicial review of the decisions to discharge them from the. armed forces. Four men were discharged on the sole ground of sexual orientation. All were devastated by their discharge. High Court dismissed the application for judicial review. Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. He considered that the balance of argument clearly lay with the applicants. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, ‘I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise’ He concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied. Simon Brown LJ also found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals into the forces. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom’S obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. It followed that the applications had to be rejected “albeit with hesitation and regret”. But the Court is bound to act with some reticence. Our approach must reflect, not overlook, where responsibility ultimately lies for the defence of the realm. In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to ‘management’ levels in the armed forces relating to the policy against homosexuals in those forces. The applicants in the judicial review proceedings had argued that the Ministry’s position was “bereft of factual evidence’ The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal on 3 November 1995. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment (with which the two other judges of the Court of appeal agreed) The more substantial the interference with human rights, the more the court will require by way of justification before it is satisfied that the decision is reasonable in the sense outlined above. Master of the Rolls says it is not the role of the courts to regulate conditions of service in the armed forces. He says the court has the constitutional role and duty of ensuring that the rights of citizens are not abused by the unlawful exercise of executive power. The court must properly defer to the expertise of responsible decision-makers, but it must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people’ He concludes that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed Forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed. Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls. He held that to dismiss a person from his or her employment on the grounds of a private sexual preference would not appear to show respect for that person’s private and family life. He questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights with which the primary adjudicating role on the Convention lay. Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments and, in particular, with the views expressed on the rationality test to be applied and on its application in the particular case. The applicants’ challenge to the arguments in support of the policy was ‘completely persuasive’ The policy was, in his view, “ripe for review and for consideration of its replacement by a strict conduct code’ Mr Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. Mr Beckett requested the withdrawal of his Industrial Tribunal proceedings and those proceedings were dismissed on 25 April 1996. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the. withdrawal of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed by the Industrial. Tribunal.

The case originated in two applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The applications were joined to two similar applications (nos. 33985/96 and 33986/96, Smith v. the United Kingdom and Grady v the United UK) The Government, represented by Mr M. Eaton and, subsequently, by Mr C. Whomersley, submitted their observations on 17 October 1997. On 17 January 1998 the Commission decided to adjourn the applications pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) The applications were examined by the Court following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 on 1 November 1998. The High Court delivered its judgment withdrawing its reference of the above question given the decision of the ECJ in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins (13 July 1998). On 4 May 1999 the President of the Chamber decided to grant Mr Lustig-Prean legal aid. The hearing in this case and in the cases of Smith and Grady v the United Kingdom took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Eadie, Counsel. The first applicant joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. The applicant was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately twenty minutes. He then confirmed that he was homosexual, acknowledging that he had been a practising homosexual since his teenage years. He was then asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject), what type of sexual relations he had. had with a particular person, when and where this had occurred, about his current relationship and whether his parents knew of his homosexuality. An anonymous letter alleged that the applicant had had a relationship with a serviceman. The applicant was asked whether he had had the relationship as alleged in the letter. His commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000). His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. The second applicant joined the Royal Navy, enlisting for twenty-two years’ service. In 1991 he became a substantive weapons engineering mechanic. He was discharged from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995. The applicant’s report dated 27 November 1992 noted that he displayed potential in a number of areas essential to good leadership, that he had the ability to become an above-average leading hand. If he applied his new skills wisely he could, with experience, be considered as a potential officer candidate. In May 1993 the applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) and consequently he spoke with the chaplain, to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. The applicant was then called for interview by the service police. He was cautioned in the same terms as the first applicant and told he would not be questioned on the above admissions prior to a search of his locker. The service police report completed after the applicant’s interview included several internal documents where it was noted that the applicant, in openly declaring his homosexuality and his relationship with a civilian, had effectively disposed “of any immediate potential security concern” For that reason, it was considered in the report that “no cause was identified for conducting a security interview with Beckett” That report also accepted that a case for fraudulent entry into the armed forces would be inappropriate given the date when the applicant had discovered his homosexuality. The applicants’ judicial review proceedings (R.C. v. Ministry of Defence, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) All four of the applicants had exemplary service records, some with reports written in glowing terms. In none of the cases before him was it suggested that the applicants’ sexual orientation had in any way affected their ability to carry out their work or had any ill-effect on discipline. There was no reason to doubt that, but for their discharge, they would have continued to perform their service duties entirely efficiently and with the continued support of their colleagues. All were devastated by their discharge. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer. Simon Brown LJ also found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals into the armed services. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that the days of the policy were numbered. The applications had to be rejected “albeit with hesitation and regret”. The court would not, for example, be inclined to overlook some minor flaw in the decision-making process, or to adopt a particularly benevolent view of the Minister's evidence. In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to ‘management’ levels in the armed forces. The paper referred to two incidents which were considered damaging to unit cohesion. The first involved a homosexual who had had a relationship with a sergeant’s mess waiter. The other involved an Australian on secondment whose behaviour was described as “so disruptive’ that his attachment was terminated. On 3 November 1995 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment (with which the two other judges of the Court. of Appeal agreed) The Master of the Rolls noted that the case concerned innate qualities of a very personal kind. He considered that the greater the policy content of the decision and the more remote the subject matter of a decision from ordinary judicial experience, the more hesitant the court had to be in holding a decision to be irrational. However, he concluded that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed in this case. He also noted that while the court must properly defer to the expertise of responsible decision-makers, it must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people’ Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls and with the latter’s approach to the irrationality test. He questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights with which the primary adjudicating role on the Convention lay. He also found that the Equal Treatment Directive did not apply to complaints in relation to sexual orientation. Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments and, in particular, with the views expressed on the rationality test to be applied and on its application in the particular case. Mr Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. Those proceedings were adjourned pending the above-described application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords. Mr Beckett requested the withdrawal of his Industrial Tribunal proceedings and those proceedings were dismissed on 25 April 1996. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the withdraw of his proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed by the Industrial tribunal. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the applicants and ordered the Secretary of State to change the law.

name: Geoffrey Twizell
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25379/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) by a British national, Mr Geoffrey Twizell (‘the applicant’), on 7 June 2002. The applicant was born in 1941 and lives in France. His wife died on 26 March 2001. His claim for widows’ benefits under the new system in place as from 9 April 2001 was made on 4 May 2001 and was rejected on 4 June 2001. On 10 July 2001 the applicant appealed. On 15 November 2001 his appeal was heard and dismissed by an Appeal Tribunal.

The case was brought by Mr Geoffrey Twizell against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1941 and lives in France. His wife died on 26 March 2001 and he had no children from the marriage. His claim for widows’ benefits under the new system in place as from 9 April 2001 was made on 4 May 2001 and was rejected on 4 June 2001 on the ground that he was not entitled to widows' benefits. On 10 July 2001 the applicant appealed. On 15 November 2001 his appeal was heard and dismissed by an Appeal Tribunal.

The case originated in an application (no. 25379/02) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Geoffrey Twizell (‘the applicant’), on 7 June 2002, made the application. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. By a decision of 12 November 2002 the Court decided to communicate the application to the President of the Chamber to which the case had been allocated. Subsequently, under the provisions of Article 29 of the convention, the President decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

His claim for widows’ benefits under the new system in place as from 9 April 2001 was made on 4 May 2001 and was rejected on 4 June 2001. On 10 July 2001 the applicant appealed. Reconsideration took place on 23 July 2001 and the decision remained unchanged.

name: Ludwig Weh
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38544/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, inter alia, that the first applicant's right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself had been breached in criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The Government filed observations on the admissibility and merits. By a decision of 4 July 2002 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1) and the judgment was published on 6 August 2002. The applicant, Mr W. Weh, was born in 1952 and lives in Bregenz. He was ordered to pay 800 Austrian schillings for exceeding the speed limit by 21 km/h. He did not comply with the anonymous order and the order became invalid. The applicant appealed to the Vorarlberg Independent Administrative Panel (Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat) The panel dismissed his appeal and ordered him to pay a fine of ATS 900 (with 24 hours' imprisonment in default) The appeal was dismissed on 15 April 1996 and he was sentenced to ATS 90 by way of contribution to the costs of the proceedings. The applicant was not prosecuted for exceeding the speed limit. He lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) The Administrative Court refused to deal with the applicant's complaint since the amount of the penalty did not exceed ATS 10,000, and no important legal problem was at stake. The applicant was ordered to pay ATS 180 by way of contribution to the costs of the appeal proceedings. The University of Texas had 14 different locations in Texas. Therefore, the Panel observed that the information provided by the first applicant had indeed been inaccurate. The Panel noted that the relevant sentence of section 103 § 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act has the rank of constitutional law.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22182/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. name: Cengiz Polat
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 6 November 2006. The applicant was convicted as charged by the Istanbul State Security Court and sentenced to life imprisonment in 2000. He is currently detained in the Edirne F-type Prison in Istanbul. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code. The case was quashed by the Court of Cassation for procedural reasons in 2001. name: Mats Eriksson
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the administrative courts had failed to hold an oral hearing in proceedings relating to his request for life annuity. On 2 February 2011 the application was communicated to the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden. The case was heard by Mr Mats Eriksson (“the applicant’s” lawyer) and Ms G. Isaksson, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The judge found against the applicant and ordered the Government to pay him an early retirement pension from 1 December 2001. The applicant’s legal counsel appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Södermanland, claiming that the applicant had a right to a life annuity since his illnesses had been work-related. At times he had had up to three different jobs, each one of which, had been hectic and thereby created a difficult and very stressful situation. In reaching its decision, the court had regard to the medical certificates by Dr B.M., which established no link between the work situation and the applicant's illness, as well as the medical opinion by Dr. C-G.E. which suggested that there existed such a link. The applicant asked for an oral hearing to deal with his case as a whole, including the question of leave to appeal. He also wanted to be heard himself about his work situation and the stressful environment. The court asked the applicant to complete his written submissions. On 29 October 2007 the Supreme Administrative Court rejected the request. The case is currently pending at the European Court of Human Rights. The application is currently before the International Court of Justice in Strasbourg, which is expected to hear the case within the next few weeks. The applicant’s legal team has asked for the case to be adjourned until at least the end of September. Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal. Court found no reason to hold an oral hearing. The applicant was requested to complete his written submissions. The court noted that leave to Appeal was granted if the case was a precedent case or if serious material or procedural mistakes were involved. As this was not so in the present case, the court found no reasons to try the case on its merits. The case was dismissed on the grounds that it did not meet the legal requirements to be heard by the Court of Appeal. The appeal was dismissed and the applicant was ordered to pay a fine of £2,000. The decision was made on 27 May 2008.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the administrative courts had failed to hold an oral hearing in proceedings relating to his request for life annuity. On 2 February 2011 the application was communicated to the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden by Ms Isaksson, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The Government was represented by Mr R. Helenius, a lawyer practising in Jönköping. The application was heard on 13 November 2008. It was settled on 13 December 2008. The case was heard by Mr Mats Eriksson, a Swedish national. The applicant’s legal counsel appealed to the County Administrative Court of the County of Södermanland, claiming that the applicant had a right to a life annuity since his illnesses had been work-related. At times he had had up to three different jobs, each one of which, had been hectic and thereby created a difficult and very stressful situation. He produced a medical opinion by Dr. C-G.E., dated 5 February 2003, which stated that known risk factors for arteriosclerosis and heart attack were, among other factors, diabetes, smoking and high blood pressure. The feeling of severe stress, especially over a long period of time, has been shown to be an element that increased the risk of developing heart and vascular disorders. The applicant asked to be heard before the court about the existence of a causal link between his work and his injury. The Administrative Court of Appeal rejected the request for an oral hearing, finding that there was no reason to hold one to decide on the question of leave to appeal. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten), reiterating the grounds of appeal already presented before the lower instances. The application was rejected on 29 October 2007 and the applicant appealed again to the High Court of Justice. The appeal was denied again on 8 March 2009. The case is now before the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal. Court found no reason to hold an oral hearing. The applicant was requested to complete his written submissions. Court ruled there was no case to be tried on the merits of the appeal. The case was settled by a jury in 2007, and the appeal was dismissed in April 2008. The appeal was heard by the Supreme Administrative Court on 27 May 2008, but the case was not heard by a judge at that time. The decision was made by a three-judge panel. The Appeal Court ruled that the appeal should be dismissed on the grounds that there was not enough evidence to try the case on its merits.

name: Juan Manuel Palomo Sánchez
train_texts: The case originated in six applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr L. García Quinteiro, a lawyer practising in Barcelona. The Spanish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr F. Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 17 November 2009 the Chamber, composed of Josep Casadevall, President, Elisabet Fura, Corneliu Bîrsan, Alvina Gyulumyan, Egbert Myjer, Luis López Guerra and Ann Power, judges, and Santiago Quesada, Section Registrar, decided to join the proceedings in the applications. The applicants sought to secure recognition by their employer of their special “salaried worker’s status” The applicants set up the trade union Nueva Alternativa Asamblearia (NAA) to defend their interests and those of the other delivery staff who were under pressure from the company P. to renounce their claim to salaried status. The applicants and the Government filed memorials before the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 December 2010 (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel, and for the applicants Mr L. García Quinteiro, lawyer, Counsel. The applicants joined the union’s executive committee. No changes concerning the appointment of the union members or their duties have taken place since the union was formed. The union NAA published a monthly newsletter. On the cover of the newsletter, a cartoon with speech bubbles showed a caricature of the human resources manager, G., sitting behind a desk under which a person on all fours could be seen from behind. Inside the newsletter were two articles which vehemently denounced the fact that those two individuals had testified in favour of the company P. in proceedings that the applicants had brought against their employer. The applicants challenged that decision before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 17, which dismissed their claims and found that the dismissals were justified. The first article contained caricatures of A. and B., showing them gagged by a handkerchief tied behind their heads. The text underneath read as follows: “We knew who they were and how they behaved, but we didn’t know how far they were prepared to go in order to hold onto their seats and cushy jobs without doing anything” The text was a response to what had happened during proceedings brought by the applicants before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 13, in which A and B. had appeared as witnesses against the applicants’ interests and in favour of their employer. The article entitled “When you’ve rented out your arse you can’n shit when you please” read as following: ‘If you belong to a works council and you have to sign agreements with your employers that will never be honoured, just to keep you quiet, and agree to changes that only benefit their cronies, and to pay cuts and other sell-outs’ You can see the injustices meted out on your colleagues, but say nothing, for fear of drawing attention to yourself. You’re fed up with your work, pissed off, anxious, stressed and in despair, because of the longer working hours and the responsibilities, products, promotions and pressures. You could break everything up, tear it to pieces, crush and demolish it all ... but your hands are tied by credits, IOUs and debts. You are crushed by your new SUV, your children’s after-school activities, and the twenty-five year mortgage on your semi-detached house. You let yourself be humiliated, you swallow your pride, you shut up and you accept, because when you’ve rented out your arse, you can’t shit when you please. The High Court of Justice of Catalonia upheld the judgment under appeal in so far as it concerned the applicants. The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, seeking harmonisation of the relevant case-law. In a decision of 11 March 2004, the Supreme Court of Spain ruled that the dismissal of the applicants by the company was based on serious misconduct as provided for by law. The court referred, among other things, to the limits imposed by the principle of good faith between parties to a contract of employment and to the necessary balance that judicial decisions had to strike between a worker’s obligations under the contract and his freedom of expression. For the court, the publication of the offending drawing and articles had clearly been harmful to the dignity of the persons concerned. The applicants lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. The Constitutional Court found the appeal inadmissible for lack of constitutional content. In their allegations, the appellants have simply expressed their disagreement with the decisions rendered by the courts below. In line with what this court has repeatedly said, such evidence does not consist of a mere allegation of a constitutional violation but must be sufficient for it to be inferred that the violation could have been constituted. The circumstances alleged do not give rise to any suspicion as to the potential violation in question. As the Court held recently in judgment no. 39/2005 of 28 February (legal ground 4), reiterating its case-law, the Constitution does not prohibit the use of hurtful, embarrassing or vituperative expressions in every circumstance. The Court finds that the appellants’ right to freedom of expression has not been infringed. “They used that right in an excessive manner by means of value judgments expressed through cartoons and comments that were offensive and humiliating for the persons concerned and impugned their honour and reputation,” the court said. The protection afforded by Article 20. 1 (a) of the Constitution does not, however, extend to absolutely vexatious expressions which, taking. into account the actual circumstances of the case and regardless of their veracity or. lack of veracity, are offensive or defamatory. The application of that jurisprudence to the present case leads the. Court to the conclusion that the. right tofreedom of expression is not infringed, since they used that. right in a excessive manner.

The case originated in six applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr L. García Quinteiro, a lawyer practising in Barcelona. The Spanish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr F. Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 11 December 2008 the President of the Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. On 17 November 2009 the Chamber, composed of Josep Casadevall, Elisabet Fura, Corneliu Bîrsan, Alvina Gyulumyan, Egbert Myjer, Luis López Guerra and Ann Power, judges, decided to join the proceedings in the applications. The applicants and the Government filed memorials before the Grand Chamber. The applicants sought to secure recognition by their employer of their special ‘salaried worker’ status. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 December 2010. The Court heard addresses by them but did not issue a verdict. The Government was represented by Mr F. Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel, Agent; the applicants by Mr L. García Quinteiro, lawyer, Counsel. It was decided that there had been no violation of Article 10 of the Convention and that no separate question arose under Article 11. The applicants joined the union’s executive committee. No changes concerning the appointment of the union members or their duties have taken place since the union was formed. The union published a monthly newsletter. On the cover of the newsletter, a cartoon with speech bubbles showed a caricature of the human resources manager, G., sitting behind a desk under which a person on all fours could be seen from behind. The applicants challenged that decision before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 17, which, in a judgment of 8 November 2002, dismissed their claims and found that the dismissals were justified. The company notified the applicants of their dismissal on grounds of serious misconduct, namely for impugning the reputations of the applicants. The first article, entitled “Whose witnesses? Theirs, of course’, contained caricatures of A. and B., showing them gagged by a handkerchief tied behind their heads. The text underneath read as follows: “We knew who they were and how they behaved, but we didn’t know how far they were prepared to go in order to hold onto their seats and cushy jobs without doing anything” The tribunal noted that the text was a response to what had happened during proceedings brought by the applicants before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 13, in which the applicants had appeared as witnesses against the applicants’ interests and in favour of their employer. The newsletter was distributed to staff and displayed on the trade union’s noticeboard on the company's premises. The employment tribunal observed at the outset that the cause of the dismissal was the content of the newsletter and not the applicants’ trade-union membership. It referred in its judgment to the exercise of the right to freedom of expression in the context of labour relations and to the fact that it was not unlimited. It found that the limits to this right had to be interpreted in accordance with the principle of good faith, which in labour relations had to involve respect for the interests of the employer and the minimum requirements of coexistence. The tribunal took the view that the cartoon and speech bubbles on the cover, together with the articles inside, were offensive and exceeded the limits of freedom of expression and information. The court referred, among other things, to the limits imposed by the principle of good faith between parties to a contract of employment. The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, seeking harmonisation of the relevant case-law. In a decision of 11 March 2004, the Supreme Court of Catalonia upheld the judgment under appeal in so far as it concerned the applicants. The company P. had, moreover, duly shown that the applicants’ dismissal was not a measure of reprisal or punishment, but was based on a genuine, serious and sufficient cause. Appellants’ dismissal was an act of reprisal on the part of the respondent company because of the judicial proceedings they had brought against it to assert their rights. The Constitutional Court found the appeal inadmissible for lack of constitutional content. In line with what this court has repeatedly said, such evidence does not consist of a mere allegation of a constitutional violation but must be sufficient for it to be inferred that the violation could have been constituted. In their allegations, the appellants have simply expressed their disagreement with the decisions rendered by the courts below. The Court held recently in judgment no. 39/2005 of 28 February (legal ground 4), reiterating its case-law, that the Constitution does not prohibit the use of hurtful, embarrassing or vituperative expressions.  constitutional protection afforded by Article 20 § 1 (a) of the Constitution does not, however, extend to absolutely vexatious expressions. The Court concluded that the appellants’ right to freedom of expression has not been infringed. “They used that right in an excessive manner by means of value judgments expressed through cartoons and comments that were offensive and humiliating for the persons concerned and impugned their honour and reputation,” the court said in its decision. The decision was made on the basis of the jurisprudence of the Supreme Court of Appeal, which upheld the right to free speech in the context of a trade-union.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the lack of legal assistance to the applicant during his police custody to the Government. The applicant was detained at a gendarme station, where he was questioned in the absence of a lawyer and his detailed statement was recorded verbatim. He was charged with the offence of carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. He sought the death penalty under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. He is serving his prison sentence in the Gaziantep H-type Prison. The applicant was sentenced to death by the Diyarbakır State Security Court. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. The applicant was represented by his lawyer. He told the court that he had joined the PKK in 1995 and had received military training. He further admitted to certain charges brought against him. The court found it established, on the basis of, inter alia, the statements taken from the applicant after his arrest and the testimony given by him during the trial. He had been involved in the killing and kidnapping of a number of village guards.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4789/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that there had been a violation of Article 8, taken separately or together with Article 14, on account of the refusal by the national authorities to indicate her forename in the civil register of births as that of the mother of her adopted child. She argued that in relation to single-parent adoptions there was a lacuna in the Civil Code which required the court to make provision for such a situation. The application was dismissed. The court dismissed the applicant’s request on the ground that it had no legal basis. It found that the Civil Code, in choosing to regulate only two-parent adoptions, intended to treat the legal relationship between the adoptive parents and the adopted child as ‘a biological relationship’ On 15 March 2009, a new regulation entered into force entitled “Regulation on the implementation of mediation services for the adoption of minors” (“the Regulation”) enabling a single adoptive parent to have his or her forename registered in the place of that of the biological parent. That request was granted on the same day and the record entries concerning the child were consequently amended.

name: Leyla Şahin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 44774/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that a ban on wearing the Islamic headscarf in higher-education institutions violated her rights and freedoms. By a decision of 2 July 2002 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Court heard addresses by Mr Grosz, Mr Alpaslan and Mr Güran. Both the applicant (on 21 November 2002, 9 May, 4 July and 25 September 2003) and the Government (on 5 and 18 March, 7 and 13 November 2003) lodged written observations and observations. The woman in question was wearing a headscarf when she attended the University of Bursa. She was not allowed to leave the university unless she had a doctor's note. The woman was also banned from attending lectures without a doctor’s note. She also had to wear a head-covering when she went out for a walk in the rain. The ban was imposed on all students wearing headscarfs, even if they were only wearing their hair. She has since been allowed to return to the university. She said she is happy to wear the headwear when she goes out for walks. She says she feels like she is doing her civic duty by wearing the headpiece. The application for an order setting aside the circular of 23 February 1998 was dismissed in March 1999. name: Waleria Kroenitz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 77746/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mrs Waleria Kroenitz, is a Polish national, who was born in 1903 and lives in Przemyśl, Poland. In 1948 the applicant’s property was expropriated. On 28 June 1996 the Minister of Economy (Minister Gospodarki) annulled the expropriation order. On 23 December 1996 the applicant brought a claim against a company “Domgos” before the Częstochowa Regional Court. The court held hearings on 30 May, 10 July and 17 October 1997. On 8 March 1999 the Częstochowa Regional Court held a hearing and gave an interlocutory judgment. It ordered that the property be restored to the applicant. On 8 March 2002 the Regional Court gave judgment and awarded the applicant compensation. Following the defendant’s appeal, the proceedings are pending before the Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny).B. Proceedings concerning a claim for compensation against the State Treasury against the Minister of Economy. The applicant's appeal is still pending at the Court for Appeal, Warsaw. The defendant's appeal to have her compensation awarded is pending.

name: James Malone
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8691/79) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission on 19 July 1979. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8 and 13 (art. 8, art. 13) of the Convention. Mr. Malone stated that he wished to participate in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Sir Vincent Evans, the elected judge of British nationality. The Post Office Engineering Union (‘the POEU’) requested leave under Rule 37 para. 2 to submit written comments, indicating, inter alia, its “specific occupational interest’ in the case and five themes it would want to develop in written comments. The President of the Court directed that the oral proceedings should open on 20 February 1984 (Rule 38). The comments should bear solely on certain of the matters referred to in the list of proposed themes and then only “in so far as such matters relate to the particular issues of alleged violation of the Convention which are before the Court for decision in the Malone case’. Hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 February. James Malone was charged with a number of offences relating to dishonest handling of stolen goods. His trial, which took place in June and August 1978, resulted in his being acquitted on certain counts and the jury disagreeing on the rest. He was retried on the remaining charges between April and May 1979. Following a further failure by the jury to agree, he was once more formally arraigned; the prosecution offered no evidence and he was acquitted. In 1977, Mr. Malone was an antique dealer. It appears that he has since ceased business as such. Malone v. Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis (No. 2), [ 1979] 2 All England Law Reports 620; also reported at [1979] 2 Weekly Law Reports 700. It was admitted by the Government that the single conversation about which evidence emerged at the applicant’s trial had been intercepted on behalf of the police pursuant to a warrant issued under the hand of the Secretary of State for the prevention and detection of crime. According to the Government, this interception was carried out in full conformity with the law and the relevant procedures. No disclosure was made either at the trial of the applicant or during the course of the. proceedings against the Metropolitan Police Commissioner. Mr Malone claimed that his telephone had been “metered’ on behalf of the police by a device which automatically records all numbers dialled. As evidence for this belief, he asserted that when he was charged in March 1977 the premises of about twenty people whom he had recently telephoned were searched by the police. The Government affirmed that the police had neither caused the applicant’s telephone calls to be metered nor undertaken the alleged or any search operations on the basis of any list of numbers obtained from metering. been intercepted. The Post Office and the police both replied that they had no authority in the matter. In September 1978, the applicant requested the Post Office to remove suspected listening devices from his telephone.

name: Celal Çağlar
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11181/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant signed a contract with POAŞ (Petrol Ofisi A.Ş.), formerly a State-owned enterprise, for the operation of a petrol station. Having obtained a construction permit and carried out certain building work at the site, the applicant applied for an operations licence but was refused on grounds of safety, due to the proximity of the petrol station to a railway. The Court rejected the request for the reimbursement of the applicant's remaining expenditure. The applicant's case was joined to the initial case (no. 1997/305) The Ankara Commercial Court partially granted the applicant's requests and awarded him TRL 5,138,188,500 for the expenses incurred in relation to the construction work. The Court of Cassation partially quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on account of the insufficient factual examination of the alleged additional financial loss. The applicant subsequently recovered from the POAŞ the total amount of 222,910 new Turkish liras TRY; (approximately 100,000 euros; EUR), which included approximately EUR 95,000 for the late return of the guarantee paid by the applicant in 1995.

The applicant was represented by Ms Tuğba Çağlar, a lawyer practising in Trabzon. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The parties requested rectification of the first-instance court's decision. The President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applicant's application at the same time. On 21 August 2002 the applicant lodged a further complaint with the Ankara Commercial Court under Article 105 of the Code of Obligations alleging that he had sustained additional loss exceeding the late-payment interest payable as a result of the delay in reimbursing the guarantee (case no. 2002/567). The applicant subsequently recovered from the POAŞ the total amount of 222,910 new Turkish liras TRY; (approximately 100,000 euros; EUR), which included approximately EUR 95,000 for the late return of the guarantee.

name: Ivan Hooper
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42317/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that neither he nor his legal representative were given the opportunity to address the magistrates' court prior to the imposition of a binding over order. By a decision of 21 October 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was decided in favour of the applicant and against the UK Government by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in October 2003. The ECJ ruled that the application was not admissible under Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was “bound over” in his own recognisance of 50 pounds sterling (GBP) together with a surety of GBP 250. The precise terms of the order were found by the Divisional Court (in the later judicial review proceedings) to be unclear. The applicant was committed to custody on the same day for 28 days. On 2 June 1997 the applicant was granted leave to apply for judicial review of the decision to impose the binding over order. The application was successful on 20 January 1998. The judges agreed that the order had been procedurally irregular and granted a declaration to that effect. During the course of their judgments, the judges held that: (a) previous domestic case-law had established that there were circumstances where failing to hear a defendant or his representative prior to the order was unlawful. Mr Justice Mance said it was a breach of the rules of natural justice to bind a person over without inquiring into his means. A surety required the separate approval of the court as to his suitability. The High Court accepted that the applicant's representative was effectively presented with a “fait accompli” of a nature which she had not come across before. The magistrates' court did not expressly invite or give opportunity for any submissions, or indeed any discussion between the applicant and his representative, about the proposed terms of the binding over order before he imposed it. The judge said the advocate's representative does not appear to have had the confidence to do so. Mr Justice Mance stated that it cannot be shown that it would have made any difference if the magistrate had given to the applicant [and his counsel] an opportunity to make representations. Mr Burnett did not seek to controvert that. However, it seems to me certainly not beyond the bounds of possibility, that if a proper opportunity had been given to [the applicant's counsel] to consider and address the matter. The magistrate might, in such circumstances, have been persuaded to a different result. This is all, of course, speculative, but speculation though it may be, the reason why it is speculation is that the magistrate failed, in my judgment, to give the applicant or, on his behalf, [ the applicant's representative] proper time to address the terms of the proposed bind over order.”

The application was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that neither he nor his legal representative were given the opportunity to address the magistrates' court prior to the imposition of a binding over order. He was later committed to prison for failure to comply with its terms. By a decision of 21 October 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was settled in favour of the applicant and the UK Government in November 2003. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998 when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The applicant was “bound over” in his own recognisance of 50 pounds sterling (GBP) together with a surety of GBP 250. The magistrate did not give any opportunity for the applicant or his representative to make submissions about the terms of the order before it was imposed. On 2 June 1997 the applicant was granted leave to apply for judicial review of the decision to impose the binding over order. The Divisional Court (Lord Justice Simon Brown and Mr Justice Mance) agreed that thebinding over order had been procedurally irregular and granted a declaration to that effect. The applicant was committed to custody on the same day for 28 days. During the course of their judgments, the judges of the Divisional court held that there were circumstances where failing to hear a defendant and his representative prior to imposing the order was a breach of natural justice. Mr Justice Mance said the magistrate did not have the confidence of the applicant's representative. The High Court accepted that the applicant was effectively presented with a ‘fait accompli’ of a nature which she had not come across before. The judge said it was a breach of the rules of natural justice for a court to bind a person over without inquiring into his means and giving him an opportunity to make representations as to the size of the recognisance. He added that magistrates needed to take particular care lest, in effect, they imposed a binding order which amounted to an automatic sentence of imprisonment without appreciating what they were doing. Mr Justice Mance stated that it cannot be shown that it would have made any difference if the magistrate had given to the applicant [and his counsel] an opportunity to make representations. Mr Burnett did not seek to controvert that. However, it seems to me certainly not beyond the bounds of possibility, that if a proper opportunity had been given to [the applicant's counsel] to consider and address the matter. The magistrate might, in such circumstances, have been persuaded to a different result. This is all, of course, speculative, but speculation though it may be, the reason why it is speculation is that the magistrate failed, in my judgment, to give the applicant or, on his behalf, [ the applicant's representative] proper time to address the terms of the proposed bind over order.”

On 20 January 1998 theDivisional Court granted the application for judicialreview. The judges agreed that the bindingover order had been procedurally irregular and granted a declaration to that effect. Mr Justice Mance said it could amount to a breach of the rules of natural justice. A surety required the separate approval of the court as to his suitability. name: Ingo Hentschel
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47274/15) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants alleged that they had been beaten and that pepper spray had been used on them by police officers who, owing to an inadequate investigation, had been neither identified nor punished. On 26 February 2016 the application was communicated to the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany. The application was brought by two German nationals, Mr Ingo Hentschel and Mr Matthias Stark, who went to a football match in Munich in December 2007. The police had predicted an increased risk of clashes between rival football supporters. Police cordoned off the stands of the supporters of one of the teams. The first applicant was hit with a truncheon on the head, which resulted in a bleeding laceration of 3 cm behind his ear. Both applicants were able to identify their attackers as police officers, but were not able to distinguish them further, owing to their identical uniforms and the lack of identifying signs or name tags. Both uniforms did not include any name tags or other signs identifying the individual officers. However, on the back of the helmets an identification number of the squad was displayed. After a few minutes the police pacified the situation and got the exiting spectators out of the stadium. Munich public prosecutor’s office instigated a preliminary investigation. First applicant filed a criminal complaint against an unidentified police officer on 25 April 2008. Several other spectators at the match had also lodged criminal complaints against unidentified police officers. On 10 September 2008 the competent public prosecutor discontinued the investigation. He found that some of the police officers had used truncheons against spectators, including women and children, in a disproportionate way and without an official order or approval. However, he concluded that the investigation had not led to a situation where concrete acts of violence could be related to specific police officers and that there was no credible evidence of this. The applicants appealed against the decision to discontinue the investigation. A further twenty-two witnesses were interviewed including 14 platoon leaders, squad leaders and video officers of the deployed police units. The individual squad members of the three squads of the Munich riot control unit were not interviewed. The applicants had requested that they be interviewed, as the evidence had suggested that the alleged perpetrators had belonged to one of these three squads. The investigating police unit was also provided with video surveillance recorded by the 23rd platoon of the 6th Dachau public-order support force battalion. Upon the request of the applicants to secure the entire video material of the police operation, it was established that the original video tapes and possible digital copies had already been deleted. Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible. The applicants lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 2, 19, 4 and 103 of the German Basic Law. The court interpreted the application as a request to force criminal proceedings (Klageerzwingungsantrag) and held that these proceedings were only admissible if the prosecution of one or more identified accused had been requested. Only in a case where a public prosecutor’s office had entirely refrained from investigating a crime had a court the possibility to order an investigation. Under Article 173 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozessordnung) a court was only allowed to conduct minor enquiries to fill in remaining gaps in an Investigation. The Federal Constitutional Court refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. A subsequent appeal before the Munich general public prosecutor was to no avail. The investigation against the five police officers was discontinued by the Munich public prosecutor’s office. The applicants alleged that several relevant parts of the video material, showing disproportionate police violence, had been deleted. In its decision the Constitutional Court referred to the case-law concerning the procedural obligation of Article 2 of the Convention and, in particular, to the cases of McCann and Others v the United Kingdom (27 September 1995, Series A no. 324) and Grams v Germany ((dec., no. 33677/96, ECHR 1999‑VII)

name: Hasan Şentürk
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 27577/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Hasan Şentürk (“the applicant”) was taken into police custody on suspicion of armed robbery and murder. On 27 October 1996 he was placed in detention on remand. On 29 June 2001 the Bursa Assize Court acquitted the applicant of the charges against him and this judgment was upheld by the Court of Cassation on 19 March 2002. The applicant was awarded 358,071,000 Turkish liras (TRL) for pecuniary damage and TRL 3,000,00,000 for non-pecuniary damages. On 10 August 2004 the Treasury objected to the interest rate. The case was to determine the exact amount and interest rate to be paid by the Treasury. On 26 October 2004 the Bursa Enforcement Court dismissed the Treasury's objection. On 25 February 2005 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment. The case was then remitted to the Enforcement Court. Following a re-examination of the case, and based on an expert report, on 10 June 2005 the Enforcement court ordered an additional payment of TRL 479,450,000 to the applicant. This amount was paid in August 2005. The domestic authorities had applied an interest rate of 50% per annum between 23 January 2003 and 1 January 2004, and 15% per year from January 2004.
