name: Sultan Khan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35394/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 October 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Lord Williams of Mostyn QC, Attorney-General, Mr J. Crow, Counsel, Ms R. Collins-Rice, Ms K. Jones, Advisers, and for the applicant Mr B. Emmerson. In 1993 the applicant visited a friend, B., in Sheffield. B. was under investigation for dealing in heroin. No drugs were found on the applicant. He too was interviewed, but made no admissions. He and N. were jointly charged with offences under the Customs and Excise Management Act 1979 and the Misuse of Drugs Act 1991 and committed for trial. The trial took place in December 1993. The applicant pleaded ‘not guilty’. He was re-arraigned and pleaded guilty to being knowingly concerned in the fraudulent evasion of the prohibition on the importation of heroin. On 14 March 1994 the applicant was sentenced to three years' imprisonment. The House of Lords held that there was no right to privacy in English law. Evidence obtained in circumstances which amounted to a breach of the provisions of Article 8 of the Convention was relevant to, but not determinative of, the judge's discretion to admit or exclude such evidence. The absence of a statutory system regulating the use of surveillance devices by the police was cited as the sole cause of the case coming to the House. Lord Nolan, giving the opinion of the majority of the House, added: “The absence of such a system seems astonishing, more so in view of the statutory framework which has governed the use by the Security Service since 1989.” The applicant was discharged from prison on 11 August 1994. His release was on licence until 12 May 1995. because counsel for the respondent was able to inform us, on instructions, that the government proposes to introduce legislation covering the matter in the next session of Parliament. The case was settled at the High Court in London and the appeal was settled in the Supreme Court. The verdict was upheld and the applicant was released on licence. The appeal was dismissed and the case was dismissed on appeal. The trial was adjourned until May 11, when the Appeal Court was told that the respondent would be allowed to return to prison. The Appeal Court returned a verdict of not guilty.

The case originated in an application (no. 35394/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The Government submitted their observations on 2 March 1998. The applicant replied on 30 September 1998, after an extension of the time-limit fixed for that purpose. On 16 October 1998 the Government made comments on the applicant's observations in reply. On 24 April 1999 the Court declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to a hearing on the merits. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 October 1999. The Court heard addresses by Mr Emmerson and Lord Williams. The applicant visited a friend who was under investigation for dealing in heroin. The police obtained a tape recording of a conversation, in the course of which the applicant admitted that he had been a party to the importation of drugs by N. The trial judge ruled that the evidence was admissible. The applicant was re-arraigned and pleaded guilty to being knowingly concerned in the fraudulent evasion of the prohibition on the importing of heroin. On 14 March 1994 the applicant was sentenced to three years' imprisonment. On 27 May 1994 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against conviction but also certified, as a result of an appeal, his conviction as a drug dealer. The House of Lords held that there was no right to privacy in English law. The judge's discretion had to be exercised according to whether the admission of the evidence would render the trial unfair. The absence of a statutory system regulating the use of surveillance devices by the police was the sole cause of the case, the majority of the House said in its ruling. The ruling was made on 2 July 1996 and the case is still pending. The case was heard at the Supreme Court of England and Wales on 6 September 1996. The jury returned a verdict of guilty and sentenced the defendant to six years in prison. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 8 November 1994. The appeal was dismissed on 14 October 1994. The applicant was discharged from prison on 11 August 1994. His release was on licence until 12 May 1995. Because counsel for the respondent was able to inform us, on instructions, that the government proposes to introduce legislation covering the matter in the next session of Parliament, the application was rejected. The hearing was adjourned until September 6, 1994, when the applicant was released on licence. The case was returned to the Court of Appeal on September 10, 1994. The appeal was rejected on September 11, 1994; the appeal was upheld on September 14, 1994 and the case was quashed on September 15, 1995. The decision was returned on September 16, 1994 with the decision to quash the conviction and the appeal to be heard again on September 19, 1994 at 9am.

The case originated in an application (no. 35394/97) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The Government submitted their observations on 2 March 1998. The applicant replied on 30 September 1998, after an extension of the time-limit fixed for that purpose. On 16 October 1998 the Government made comments on the applicant's observations in reply. On 24 April 1999 the Court declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to a hearing on the merits. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 October 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Lord Williams of Mostyn QC, Attorney-General, Mr J. Crow, Counsel. The trial judge ruled that the evidence was admissible. The applicant was re-arraigned and pleaded guilty to being knowingly concerned in the fraudulent evasion of the prohibition on the importation of heroin. On 14 March 1994 the applicant was sentenced to three years' imprisonment. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against conviction but also certified, as a. case of misconduct in a public office. The trial judge conducted a hearing on the voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of the jury) as to the admissibility in evidence of the conversation recorded on the tape. The Crown accepted that without it there was no case against the applicant. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against conviction. The House of Lords dismissed the appeal on 2 July 1996. Lord Nolan: The sole cause of this case is the lack of a statutory system regulating the use of surveillance devices by the police. The absence of such a system seems astonishing, more so in view of the statutory framework which has governed the. use of such devices since 1989, and the interception of communications by the. police as well as by other agencies since 1985. The judge's discretion had to be exercised according to whether the admission of the evidence would render the trial unfair. The use at a criminal trial of material obtained in breach of the right to privacy enshrined in Article 8 did not mean that the trial would be unfair. On the facts, the trial judge had been entitled to hold that the relevant evidence was obtained, even if they constituted a breach of Article 8. The applicant was discharged from prison on 11 August 1994. His release was on licence until 12 May 1995. because counsel for the respondent was able to inform us, on instructions, that the government proposes to introduce legislation covering the matter in the next session of Parliament. The hearing was adjourned until later in the year when the applicant could apply for a new licence to serve the remainder of his sentence. The applicant was released on licence on 12 May1995. The jury was told that the respondent’s counsel had informed us that the Government was planning to introduce a law covering the issue. The case was dismissed on a technicality, and the appeal was dismissed.

name: Paul Matthew Coyne
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 16 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 25942/94) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Government expressed the view that it would not be necessary to hold oral proceedings. The Government and the Commission said there was no reason to hold a hearing. The Court decided that it would be necessary to hold an oral hearing, limited to issues under Article 50 of the Convention. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 June 1997. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr M.R. Eaton, Deputy Legal Adviser, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Eadie, Counsel, and for the applicant Mr G. Blades, Solicitor. The applicant was Paul Matthew Coyne, a non-commissioned officer in the Royal Air Force. Mr Coyne was charged, pursuant to section 70 (1) of the Air Force Act 1955, with four civilian criminal offences. The charges were connected to a false application for a bank loan. Mr Coyne pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him. He was sentenced to nine months’ detention, dismissal from the air force and reduction to the ranks. On 31 January 1994 he presented a petition against conviction and sentence. He claimed that the judge advocate had erred in his summing up of the case, that he had been wrongly convicted and that the sentence was too lenient. The court martial took place at the RAF Station, Brüggen on 26‑28 January 1994. The Court of Appeal rejected the appeal on the grounds that the sentence was excessive. The decision was not based on any grounds other than that the charge was not proven. The appeal was the result of an investigation into the charge that the officer had committed an offence against a public order. The charge against the officer was related to an alleged misconduct in public office. The officer was sentenced to two years in prison. The conviction was quashed after an appeal was made to the Court of Appeals. The case was referred to the Supreme Court of Australia by the court of appeal. The court upheld the conviction on all grounds, including the fact that the allegation was not proved by the evidence. The judge also ruled that the offence was not an act of misconduct.

name: Uğur Eşim
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 59601/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was born in 1969 and lives in İstanbul. He was severely wounded by gunshots in a clash with terrorists in 1990. In 1992 he was declared to be suffering from a permanent disability and discharged from the army. In 2004 a CT scan revealed an unidentified metallic object in the left orbital area. In 2007, the applicant was admitted to the neurosurgery department of the GATA Military Hospital and a scan revealed that he had a bullet in his head, measuring 15 x 10 mm. The Supreme Military Administrative Court, by a majority, rejected both actions as being out of time. The court held that notwithstanding the fact that the applicant had not been aware of the bullet in his head until 2007, pursuant to section 43(1) of the Supreme Military. Administrative Court Act, his compensation claims should have been lodged within five years of the incident. train_texts: The case was brought against the Republic of Turkey under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. name: Karin Andersson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29878/09) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway, in violation of their rights under Articles 6 and 8. The application was communicated to the Government on 21 May 2012. The case will be heard at the Court of Appeal on 26 June 2013. The hearing is expected to last two weeks. The verdict is expected by the end of July 2013. The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. The property owners claimed that the decision contradicted Swedish law as well as applicable European Union law, including the Habitats Directive. A number of individual property owners, including three of the applicants in the present case, petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) for a judicial review of the case and requested that the Government’s decision be quashed. The decision was overturned on 6 January 2011. NRA applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. Also applied to Environmental Court (miljödomstolen) in Umeå for permits to build two bridges. Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the petitions for a judicial review because it was not possible to determine who should be considered an interested party at that stage of the railway planning. Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, considering itself bound by the Government’s decision of 12 June 2003, the court decided to grant all the permits requested by NRA. Twelve applicants – all but Ms Holmström, Mr Härestål and Mr Höjer – appealed to the Government against the railway plan. They essentially complained of the specific stretch of the railway, invoking nuisance such as noise and vibrations affecting the enjoyment of their property. The Supreme Administrative Court, after having held a hearing in the case, rejected the petition, finding that the railway Plan was in line with the EU Habitats Directive. The court considered itself bound by the Government’s decision as to the permissibility of the project and thus limited its examination to the environmental compensation measures, as indicated by the Environmental Court of Appeal. Government’s permissibility decision was binding for the subsequent proceedings in that courts and other decision-making bodies could not examine issues that had been determined by that decision. Supreme Administrative Court further stated that, if private interests were affected by the location of a railway project, judicial review could be obtained by petitioning the court. The Government had not been obliged to review its decision of 12 June 2003 on the per Missibility of the railway project and the designation of the ‘corridor’ in which the railway could be located. These issues could not be examined in the third stage of the decision process. The court, in the instant case, should have examined all the objections presented by the appellants, including the claim that there were better alternative locations. At least ten of the applicants (including seven with houses or land situated outside the “corridor”) have received some form of compensation as a consequence of the railway construction, either for land requisitioned or for reduced residential value or market value. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values. It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation. The case continues at the European Court of Justice.
